name: 9front
summary: Independent, modernised community fork of Plan 9 from Bell Labs, offering native 64-bit x86-64 support, rewritten SATA/NVMe/USB drivers, native TLS and the hjfs journaled file system.
license: Open Source (MIT Licence with components under Lucent Public License)

content.introduction: 9front is a free operating system stemming from an independent community fork of Plan 9 from Bell Labs (Fourth Edition), created in 2011. Born of the wish of experienced developers and users to revitalise the Plan 9 ecosystem faced with the inertia of corporate development at Bell Labs, 9front aims to make the innovative concepts of Plan 9 (per-process namespaces, 9P protocol, Acme textual environment) fully operational on modern personal computers, servers and virtual machines.
content.what_is_it: Technically, 9front is not a simple repackaging or minor distribution of Plan 9: it is a stand-alone system that has deeply reworked the kernel, the build chain and the hardware drivers. While preserving the conceptual purity of Plan 9 ("everything is a file", 9P2000 protocols, private namespaces composed by `bind` and `mount`), 9front has filled the hardware and network gaps that prevented the practical use of Plan 9 in the 21st century.
content.kernel_modernization_amd64_and_hardware_: One of the major achievements of 9front is the implementation of a native and robust 64-bit architecture for **x86-64 (AMD64)** microprocessors, including the kernel, the C build chain (`6c`, `6a`, `6l`) and the entire user space. The project has entirely rewritten the hardware driver stack: support for SATA disk controllers (AHCI) and ultra-fast NVMe SSD interfaces, a complete USB stack for XHCI (USB 3.x), EHCI and UHCI controllers, drivers for Gigabit and 10-Gigabit Ethernet network controllers (Intel igb/ixgbe, Realtek), Intel/AMD CPU microcode management and support for modern UEFI-mode booting alongside the legacy BIOS.
content.storage_architecture_hjfs_and_cwfs: 9front has greatly improved the reliability of the storage layer by integrating **hjfs** (Hearn's Journaled File System) by default, a modern file system bringing block journaling and snapshot support, guaranteeing the transactional integrity of data in the face of abrupt power cuts. It also maintains **cwfs** (Cache-WORM File System), designed to create two-level hierarchical file servers (fast cache memory and immutable archive storage). The 9P protocol benefits from substantial throughput optimisations and reliable negotiation extensions.
content.modern_network_stack_tls_and_git_fs: On the network side, 9front natively integrates a contemporary cryptographic stack: full IPv6 support, implementation of the TLS/SSL encryption protocols in the kernel and user space, native SSH client and server, and NTP time synchronisation. Remarkably, the system includes the `git/fs` tool, which makes it possible to handle Git repositories as a navigable virtual 9P file system: every branch, tag or commit is explored like a standard directory. The Rio graphical environment handles the smoothing of TrueType vector fonts, and the system ships with built-in retro emulators (NES, GameBoy, x86).
content.hardware_compatibility_and_community_gov: 9front runs optimally on x86-64 laptops (notably the Lenovo ThinkPad range), recent physical desktop PCs, ARM nano-computers (Raspberry Pi 0, 1, 2, 3, 4) and all modern hypervisors (QEMU, VirtualBox, bhyve). The system is distributed under the free and permissive **MIT Licence** (with components under Lucent Public License). The project is governed collegially and independently by its community, and comes with uncompromising technical documentation reputed as such, the FQA (Frequently Questioned Answers).
content.versions_images_et_cibles_materielles: 9front publishes no numbered version in the sense of Linux distributions: the current version is identified by a build number — 11952 at the time of consultation — and distributed as ready-to-use images. The download directory associates with this version a 386 ISO image, an ISO image and an amd64 qcow2 image, an arm64 qcow2 image, as well as four images intended for ARM boards named pi, pi3, honeycomb and reform. Disk preparation is documented in section 8 of the manual: fdisk and prep for partition tables, format for marking media, mbr for booting. Plan 9 partitions use type 0x39 on a DOS table and the GUID identifier C91818F9-8025-47AF-89D2-F030D7000C2C on a GPT table, which allows coexisting with other systems on the same disk.
content.security_authentication_agent_and_trust_: 9front authentication is provided by `auth/factotum`, a user-space file system that acts as an agent for a given user and keeps keys represented by `attribute=value` pairs (user, authentication domain, protocol, secret data). The service exposes the `rpc`, `proto`, `confirm`, `needkey`, `log` and `ctl` entries; reading `ctl` returns the list of keys and returns from a secret attribute only the name followed by a question mark. The `factotum(4)` page lists the supported protocols: `p9any` as negotiation meta-protocol, `p9sk1` presented as legacy, `dp9ik` which adds resistance to password brute force and forward secrecy, then `p9cr`, `apop`, `cram`, `chap`, `mschap`, `mschapv2` and `mschap2`. The agent acts as client for processes sharing its user identifier and as server for any process; the `auth(2)` page exposes the namespace management calls (`newns`, `addns`, `amount`) and the `noworld` function, which signals membership of the `noworld` group of `/adm/users` and which `telnetd` and `ftpd` use for restricted access. The `securenet(8)` page describes an external DES encryption box protected by a four-digit PIN. These documents describe mechanisms that can be enabled; they publish neither a patch policy, nor a support period, nor a vulnerability reporting procedure.
advantages: Active and modern continuation of the distributed architecture of Plan 9 on 64-bit processors (x86-64).
Modern hardware drivers rewritten for SATA AHCI, NVMe, USB 3.x (XHCI) and Gigabit Ethernet.
hjfs journaled file system with snapshots guaranteeing data resilience.
Complete contemporary network stack integrating IPv6, native TLS/SSL and SSH client/server.
Innovative `git/fs` tool exposing Git repositories as virtual 9P file trees.
Independent community governance and permissive free MIT licence.
disadvantages: Atypical learning curve requiring mastery of the private namespace concepts and of the Acme editor.
Incompatibility with most closed software or proprietary office suites of the PC world.
Support for recent physical Wi-Fi chips still partial compared with mainstream Linux distributions.
No complex hardware 3D graphical acceleration for contemporary modern video games.
Deliberately caustic documentation (FQA) requiring good technical autonomy from the user.
who_is_it_for: Developers, engineers and computer science researchers wishing to make daily use of the power of 9P distributed systems.
Admirers of the Plan 9 philosophy looking for a functional implementation on modern PC hardware.
Programmers appreciating ultra-fast and highly configurable textual environments (Acme, Sam, rc).
Enthusiasts of alternative architectures running lightweight and independent systems under QEMU or on ThinkPads.
who_is_it_not_for: Beginner users looking for a conventional desktop system of the Windows or macOS type.
Professionals depending on specific proprietary commercial software (Adobe, Microsoft Office).
Administrators of cloud computing infrastructures requiring native Linux container orchestrators.
Modern video game players requiring recent Vulkan or DirectX graphics drivers.
content.verdict: 9front is a community fork of Plan 9. By preserving the Plan 9 architecture while adding modern hardware and cryptographic foundations (AMD64, NVMe, USB 3, TLS, git/fs), it maintains a daily-usable distribution of the Bell Labs research system.
content.origin_and_earliest_release_announcement:
The project presents itself, in its own FQA, as a fork of Plan 9 from Bell Labs launched to remedy a perceived lack of development resources devoted to Plan 9 within Bell Labs. The oldest release announcement archived on the site is dated 17 June 2011, under the archive path 2011/06/17, and is entitled "Plan 9 from the People's Front of cat-v.org (9front)". This announcement states that Plan 9 had been forked to pursue development outside Bell Labs, that the home page and the code were then hosted on Google Code, that the system could be booted from a regularly built live CD or compiled in an existing Plan 9 installation, and that discussions were held on the #cat-v channel of the irc.freenode.net network.

The archive of announcements covers the years 2011 to 2026, in annual folders. The FQA states that new versions are produced "on a regular, but unscheduled, basis" and refers to that archive; it publishes neither a schedule, nor a support period, nor an end-of-life date. The last announcement consulted is dated 2 August 2026, under the archive path 2026/08/02, and is entitled "9FRONT "THIS WAS SUPPOSED TO BE FUN" RELEASED". For these two announcements, the date comes from the archive path published by the site and not from a printed mention: the pages themselves display no date.

The FQA finally describes contributions as occasional, spread across several time zones and access providers, and refers to the project mailing list for the course of development.
content.additional_software_sources_and_contrib_:
The FQA documents the distribution of additional software in the form of 9P shares. The `9fs 9front` share makes the following directories accessible under /n/: 9front/ for the system source code, 9front.torrent for the torrent of the current ISO image, extra/ for the source code of third-party software, fqa/ for the troff sources of the FQA, hardware/ for hardware known to work with its system information, its firmwares and its manuals, and iso/ for the current ISO images.

A second official share, mounted by `9fs 9contrib`, exposes under /n/contrib/ the contribution directories maintained by users of the project; these directories are also served over HTTP at contrib.9front.org. The FQA additionally refers to a list of public 9P servers, to shithub.us, to a list of Plan 9 software, to sr.ht and to the Plan9-Archive GitHub organisation, as well as to the wiki.9front.org/extra page.

It also describes ANTS, a collection of modifications and software adding namespace manipulation capabilities, presented as based on 9front and placed under the MIT licence for the original code and under the Lucent Public License for the modifications of Bell Labs code.

These pages describe a distribution through source shares and contribution directories; they document neither a binary package manager, nor a dependency resolver, nor a signed package repository.
